description: After the bombing of Guernica, Picasso painted a black and white cry against the war. The work travels, then returns to Spain after Franco.

hero.hook: A burned Basque village, a canvas that refuses to forget.

blocks.text: **April 26, 1937**, the Basque town of Guernica was bombed during . Picasso, in Paris, responded with an immense canvas, in black and white. [[The Spanish Civil War (1936-1939)]]
*Guernica* became one of the most powerful anti-war images of the 20th century.

Since **1936**, Spain has been torn between the [[Second Spanish Republic]] and Franco's nationalists, supported by the German . Guernica's aims to terrorize. [[The Condor Legion]] [[saturation bombing]]
Picasso works quickly, on large studies. He abandons color to stick to the urgency of the testimony. The monumental format prohibits comfortable contemplation.

blocks.caption: Guernica in ruins: the news item becomes a symbol.

blocks.text: Picasso composes a chaos of bodies, horse, bull, light bulb. No color: like a newspaper front page. The monumentality forces the viewer to confront.
Disemboweled horse, mother with child, arms raised: each motif is readable without a caption. This is a grammar of civil terror, not a heroic battle.
He refused to allow the painting to go to Spain as long as Franco remained in power.
After the Universal Exhibition in Paris, *Guernica* traveled and then stayed for a long time at  in New York, protected during Franco's . He returned to Madrid in **1981**. [[MoMA]] [[Cold War]]
During the dictatorship, the painting became a political exile. His return to Spain after Franco is as much a national as an aesthetic event.

blocks.caption: Black, white, gray: war without heroism.

blocks.text: Reproduced in front of the as a warning, the work remains a [[UN]]iversal language against the massacre of civilians.
To fully understand Guernica, Picasso, you must keep one thing in mind: each technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never just decorative.
Context matters as much as style. Dates, places, sponsors, public: all this explains why a form appears at a specific moment, and not before.
Finally, legacy is measured over the long term. What we see today in museums, films or popular music still bears the traces of these inventions.
Each new war brings sad news to *Guernica*. The work functions as a warning that we can never listen enough.

Context matters as much as style. Dates, places, sponsors, public: all this explains why a form appears at a specific moment, and not before.
With Guernica, Picasso transformed a 1937 bombing into a global visual memory of total war.
